claim: Stimulated muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (M2Rs) release Gβγ subunits, which slow heart rate by activating a G protein-gated K+ channel (GIRK).
source: Stimulated muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (M2Rs) release Gβγ subunits, which slow heart rate by activating a G protein-gated K+ channel (GIRK).
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism described in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Stimulated β2 adrenergic receptors (β2ARs) release Gβγ subunits, but GIRK is not activated.
source: Stimulated β2 adrenergic receptors (β2ARs) also release Gβγ subunits, but GIRK is not activated.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in the manuscript.

claim: M2Rs catalyze Gβγ subunit release at higher rates than β2ARs, generating higher Gβγ concentrations that activate GIRK.
source: K+ currents and bioluminescence resonance energy transfer between labelled G proteins and GIRK show that M2Rs catalyze Gβγ subunit release at higher rates than β2ARs, generating higher Gβγ concentrations that activate GIRK and regulate other targets of Gβγ.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by electrophysiology and BRET experiments shown in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: The higher rate of Gβγ release is attributable to a faster G protein coupled receptor – G protein trimer association rate in M2R compared to β2AR.
source: The higher rate of Gβγ release is attributable to a faster G protein coupled receptor – G protein trimer association rate in M2R compared to β2AR.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by BRET experiments measuring Gβγ dissociation from Gα (Figure 6) and kinetic modeling (Figure 7).

claim: A rate difference in a single kinetic step accounts for specificity.
source: Thus, a rate difference in a single kinetic step accounts for specificity.
evidence: This is the central conclusion of the study, supported by kinetic modeling and experimental data.

claim: Sympathetic stimulation accelerates heart rate through activation of beta-adrenergic receptors (βARs) and the stimulatory G protein (Gαs) pathway.
source: Sympathetic stimulation accelerates heart rate through activation of beta-adrenergic receptors (βARs) and the stimulatory G protein (Gαs) pathway, while parasympathetic stimulation slows heart rate through activation of the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor M2 (M2Rs) of the inhibitory G protein (Gαi) pathway (Brodde and Michel, 1999; Gordan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: Parasympathetic stimulation slows heart rate through activation of M2Rs of the inhibitory G protein (Gαi) pathway.
source: Sympathetic stimulation accelerates heart rate through activation of beta-adrenergic receptors (βARs) and the stimulatory G protein (Gαs) pathway, while parasympathetic stimulation slows heart rate through activation of the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor M2 (M2Rs) of the inhibitory G protein (Gαi) pathway (Brodde and Michel, 1999; Gordan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: GIRK channels are targeted by the parasympathetic nervous system.
source: G protein-activated inward rectifier K+ (GIRK) channels are targeted by the parasympathetic nervous system (Loewi, 1921; Irisawa et al., 1993; Schmitt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: Acetylcholine released from the vagus nerve binds to and activates M2Rs in sinoatrial node pacemaker cells.
source: Upon stimulation, acetylcholine (ACh) released from the vagus nerve binds to and activates M2Rs in sinoatrial node (SAN) pacemaker cells, promoting the engagement of the GDP-bound G protein trimer (Gαi(GDP)βγ).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of parasympathetic control of heart rate.

claim: The activated M2R catalyzes removal of GDP from the G protein alpha subunit (Gαi), which allows intracellular GTP to bind.
source: The activated receptor catalyzes removal of GDP from the G protein alpha subunit (Gαi), which allows intracellular GTP to bind.
evidence: This is the established mechanism of GPCR-mediated G protein activation.

claim: The GTP-bound Gα (Gαi(GTP)) and the G protein beta-gamma subunit (Gβγ) dissociate from the receptor and from each other.
source: The GTP-bound Gα (Gαi(GTP)) and the G protein beta-gamma subunit (Gβγ) then dissociate from the receptor and from each other (Figure 1A) (Hilger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is the established mechanism of G protein signaling, cited from the literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The Gβγ subunit, free to diffuse on the intracellular membrane surface, binds to GIRK and causes it to open.
source: The Gβγ subunit, now free to diffuse on the intracellular membrane surface (attached by a lipid anchor), binds to GIRK and causes it to open (Sakmann et al., 1983; Soejima and Noma, 1984; Logothetis et al., 1987; Wickman et al., 1994; Krapivinsky et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: Open GIRK channels hyperpolarize the cell membrane and thus lengthen the interval between cardiac action potentials.
source: Open GIRK channels hyperpolarize the cell membrane and thus lengthen the interval between cardiac action potentials (i.e. slow the heart rate) (DiFrancesco, 1993; Schmitt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: The process is reversed by the alpha subunit, which hydrolyses GTP to GDP followed by reformation of the Gαi(GDP)βγ complex.
source: The process is reversed by the alpha subunit, which hydrolyses GTP to GDP followed by reformation of the Gαi(GDP)βγ complex.
evidence: This is the established mechanism of G protein signaling termination.

claim: Application of isoproterenol to murine SAN cells increases action potential frequency.
source: Figure 1B shows spontaneous action potentials recorded from current-clamped murine SAN cells isolated from adult mice. With application of isoproterenol (Iso), action potential (AP) frequency increased, and with ACh firing altogether ceased.
evidence: This is directly observed in the electrophysiology experiment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Application of acetylcholine to murine SAN cells causes action potential firing to cease.
source: Figure 1B shows spontaneous action potentials recorded from current-clamped murine SAN cells isolated from adult mice. With application of isoproterenol (Iso), action potential (AP) frequency increased, and with ACh firing altogether ceased.
evidence: This is directly observed in the electrophysiology experiment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both Gαi-associated and Gαs-associated pathways are activated within a single pacemaker cell.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, we could not find in the literature a demonstration of both autonomic responses in the same cell. Here we observe that both Gαi-associated (via ACh to slow heart rate) and Gαs-associated (via Iso to speed heart rate) pathways are indeed activated within a single pacemaker cell.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments in Figure 1B and 1C showing both responses in the same cell.

claim: ACh produces inward K+ current through GIRK channels in murine SAN cells.
source: Figure 1C shows a voltage-clamp experiment performed on the very same cell shown in Figure 1B. ACh produces inward K+ current through GIRK channels, which is the origin of action potential cessation in Figure 1B.
evidence: This is directly observed in the voltage-clamp experiment shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Isoproterenol does not activate GIRK in murine SAN cells even though βAR stimulation is known to generate free Gβγ subunits.
source: Iso does not activate GIRK even though βAR stimulation is known to generate free Gβγ subunits.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1C and is consistent with the literature showing that βAR stimulation generates Gβγ.

claim: Only M2R receptor stimulation activates GIRK to a large extent in HEK-293T cells expressing GIRK channels and GPCRs.
source: Figure 1D shows voltage clamp experiments in human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK-293T) cells in which GIRK channels and GPCRs were heterologously expressed. M2R is a Gαi-coupled GPCR stimulated by ACh and beta 1-adrenergic receptor (β1AR) and beta 2-adrenergic receptor (β2AR) are both Gαs-coupled GPCRs stimulated by Iso. In each experiment, agonist (ACh or Iso) is applied to reveal the level of stimulated K+ current. Only M2R receptor stimulation activates GIRK to a large extent.
evidence: This is directly observed in the voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The lack of GIRK activation by β1AR and β2AR is not due to endogenous M2Rs in HEK-293T cells.
source: This expression is not due to endogenous M2Rs in HEK-293T cells, as ACh fails to stimulate GIRK channels unless M2R is expressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the control experiment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A difference in surface expression levels of the GPCRs does not explain the differential GIRK activation.
source: A difference in surface expression levels of the GPCRs does not explain this result, as Alexa Fluor 488-labeled M2Rs and β2ARs show similar fluorescence intensity at the plasma membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the confocal microscopy experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–1C.

claim: Expressed β1AR and β2AR are functional in HEK-293T cells and capable of initiating the Gαs pathway.
source: To ensure that expressed β1AR and β2AR are indeed functional in the cells and capable of initiating the Gαs pathway, the cAMP ELIZA assay was used to measure Iso-stimulated increases in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) concentration, which is not observed in control cells and is thus dependent on the β1AR and β2AR expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cAMP ELISA assay shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Specificity persists across mammalian and insect cells.
source: Similar experiments were carried out in chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells (also mammal-derived) and Spodoptera frugiperda (Sf9) cells (insect-derived) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–1E). In each cell line only M2R receptor stimulation activates GIRK channels. These data demonstrate that specificity persists across mammalian and insect cells and is therefore a robust property of these signaling pathways.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in CHO and Sf9 cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–1E.

claim: GIRK activation does not depend on Gβγ subtypes.
source: The results also imply that GIRK activation does not depend on Gβγ subtypes, because different cell lines, particularly Sf9 cells, express subtypes of Gβγ that are distinct from those in mammals (Leopoldt et al., 1997).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that specificity is maintained in Sf9 cells, which express different Gβγ subtypes, as cited from the literature.

claim: When expressed, GIRK and the GPCR remain linked together in GIRK-GPCR concatemer constructs.
source: When expressed and analyzed using a western blot, the linked GIRK channel and GPCR run on SDS-PAGE gels as either full-length GIRK-GPCR units or as dimers, trimers and tetramers of those units (Figure 2B). Therefore, when expressed, GIRK and the GPCR remain linked together.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: M2R-GIRK concatemers show GIRK activation in response to ACh stimulation.
source: Voltage-clamp experiments on HEK-293T cells transiently transfected with the M2R-GIRK construction showed GIRK activation in response to ACh stimulation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the voltage-clamp experiment shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Iso stimulation with cells expressing the β2AR-GIRK construction did not activate GIRK.
source: Iso stimulation with cells expressing the β2AR-GIRK construction did not activate GIRK (Figure 2D), even though the β2AR is functional as evidenced by quantifying levels of stimulated cAMP (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the voltage-clamp experiment shown in Figure 2D, with functional validation in Figure 2E.

claim: The macromolecular supercomplex hypothesis does not explain Gβγ specificity.
source: These experiments do not support the macromolecular supercomplex hypothesis as an explanation for Gβγ specificity.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that enforced proximity through GPCR-GIRK concatemers does not override specificity (Figure 2).

claim: Expression of additional Gαi1 subunits suppressed the level of M2R-stimulated GIRK current.
source: In control experiments endogenous G protein levels support M2R stimulated GIRK channel activation (Figure 3A), as was observed in Figure 1. Expression of additional Gαi1 subunits suppressed the level of M2R-stimulated GIRK current, presumably because excess Gαi1 subunits blunt the normal increase in Gβγ concentration (i.e. Gαi1 can compete with the channel for available Gβγ).
evidence: This is observed in the experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of additional Gαi1 and Gβγ subunits leads to M2R-stimulated GIRK current that exceeds levels mediated by endogenous G proteins alone.
source: Expression of additional Gαi1 and Gβγ subunits, however, leads to M2R-stimulated GIRK current that exceeds levels mediated by endogenous G proteins alone (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experiments shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Increased availability of Gαi(GDP)βγ substrate leads to increased Gβγ levels following M2R stimulation.
source: This latter observation would seem to suggest that increased availability of Gαi(GDP)βγ substrate (upon which stimulated M2R acts to generate free Gβγ) leads to increased Gβγ levels following M2R stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that overexpression of Gαi1 and Gβγ increases GIRK current.

claim: Excess Gαs and Gβγ subunits give rise to β2AR-stimulated GIRK current.
source: Experiments using cells expressing GIRK channels and β2ARs show that excess Gαs and Gβγ subunits give rise to β2AR-stimulated GIRK current (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experiments shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The specificity exhibited by Gαi-coupled GPCRs versus Gαs-coupled GPCRs is related to differences in the levels of Gβγ that they each are able to generate.
source: This finding suggests that the specificity exhibited by Gαi-coupled GPCRs versus Gαs-coupled GPCRs is somehow related to differences in the levels of Gβγ that they each are able to generate.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that overexpression of G proteins can override specificity.

claim: M2R stimulation produces a robust increase in the BRET signal between Gβγ-Venus and masGRK3ct-NLuc.
source: First, we examined the binding of Gβγ-Venus to the membrane anchored C-terminal PH domain of GRK3 fused to NLuc (masGRK3ct-NLuc), which is known to bind to Gβγ with ~20 nM affinity (Pitcher et al., 1992). This experiment produced a robust increase in the BRET signal following M2R stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the BRET experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No change in BRET signal occurred following M2R stimulation when examining the binding of Gβγ-Venus to Kir2.2 fused to NLuc.
source: Second, we examined the binding of Gβγ-Venus to Kir2.2 fused to NLuc. Kir2.2 is structurally similar to GIRK but does not bind to Gβγ. No change in BRET signal occurred following M2R stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the BRET experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The BRET assay is suitable for monitoring a specific interaction between GIRK and Gβγ subunits released following GPCR stimulation.
source: These positive and negative controls imply that the BRET assay may be suitable for monitoring a specific interaction between GIRK and Gβγ subunits released following GPCR stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the positive and negative control experiments.

claim: The BRET signal showed a time-dependent increase following ACh stimulation of M2R, even in the absence of additional Gαi1.
source: HEK-293T cells were transiently transfected with M2Rs, Gβγ-Venus, GIRK-NLuc, and varying concentrations of Gαi1. The BRET signal was then monitored over time following ACh stimulation (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E). Even in the absence of additional Gαi1, the BRET signal showed a time-dependent increase, consistent with Gβγ-Venus being released from M2Rs and then binding to the GIRK channel.
evidence: This is directly observed in the BRET experiments shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: As the amount of Gαi1 expression was increased the BRET signal increased further.
source: As the amount of Gαi1 expression was increased the BRET signal increased further, consistent with more Gβγ-Venus being generated as a result of greater Gαi1(GDP)βγ-Venus substrate availability.
evidence: This is directly observed in the BRET experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: As the level of Gαi1 expression is increased a maximum BRET signal is reached.
source: As the level of Gαi1 expression is increased a maximum BRET signal is reached, suggesting that an aspect of this signaling pathway other than Gαi1 availability eventually becomes limiting.
evidence: This is observed in the BRET experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Only a very small change in the BRET signal was observed with β2AR in the absence of Gαs transfection.
source: When the same experiment was carried out with the β2AR only a very small change in the BRET signal was observed in the absence of Gαs transfection (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), consistent with the failure of β2AR stimulation (in the absence of Gαs transfection) to activate GIRK channels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the BRET experiments shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The BRET ratio increased with increased expression of Gαs for β2AR.
source: In accord with the ability of Gαs and Gβγ over-expression to over-ride specificity and permit β2AR-stimulated GIRK current (Figure 3B), the BRET ratio increased with increased expression of Gαs (and Gβγ-Venus).
evidence: This is directly observed in the BRET experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The electrophysiological and BRET assays are in complete agreement with each other.
source: The electrophysiological and BRET assays are in complete agreement with each other and suggest that specificity in Gαi-coupled GPCR signaling results from higher Gβγ concentrations achieved when Gαi-coupled receptors are stimulated compared to Gαs-coupled receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency between the electrophysiology and BRET experiments.

claim: TRPM3 channels are inhibited by Gβγ.
source: To test this idea, we carried out experiments using the transient receptor potential melastatin 3 (TRPM3) channel, which is inhibited by Gβγ (Figure 4A) (Badheka et al., 2017; Quallo et al., 2017; Dembla et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: TRPM3 channels were inhibited 85 ± 10% by stimulating M2R with Ach.
source: TRPM3 channels were first activated by a chemical ligand, pregnenolone sulphate (PS), and then inhibited (85 ± 10%) by stimulating M2R with Ach (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Iso-stimulated β2ARs showed only modest inhibition (17 ± 10%) of TRPM3 channels.
source: Similar experiments with Iso-stimulated β2ARs showed only modest inhibition (17 ± 10%), consistent with some degree of specificity as a result of there being insufficient concentrations of Gβγ generated by the Gαs-coupled pathway (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: Specificity is lost when Gαs and Gβγ are over-expressed in TRPM3 experiments.
source: As in the GIRK experiments, specificity is lost when Gαs and Gβγ are over-expressed (inhibition 73 ± 14%) (Figure 4B–4F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 4B–4F.

claim: Gαi-coupled receptors generate higher concentrations of Gβγ in the setting of endogenous G protein concentrations.
source: These observations further strengthen the idea that Gαi-coupled receptors generate higher concentrations of Gβγ in the setting of endogenous G protein concentrations and that these higher Gβγ levels account for Gβγ specificity.
evidence: This is inferred from the TRPM3 experiments showing similar specificity as GIRK.

claim: Similar Gβγ specificity is observed with a completely different protein target of the Gβγ pathway.
source: These observations also further reject the macromolecular supercomplex hypothesis as a tenable explanation, because similar Gβγ specificity is observed with a completely different protein target of the Gβγ pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TRPM3 shows similar specificity as GIRK.

claim: The endogenous levels of Gαs in HEK-293T cells are higher than Gαi.
source: This explanation seems unlikely though, because the endogenous levels of Gαs in HEK-293T cells are actually higher than Gαi when we measure levels directly using a Western blot assay in the same cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Higher levels of Gαs in HEK-293T cells were also reported previously on the basis of RNA levels.
source: Higher levels of Gαs in HEK-293T cells were also reported previously on the basis of RNA levels (Atwood et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The affinities of Gαi1(GTP-γS) and Gαs(GTP-γS) for Gβγ are similar.
source: Inhibition of GIRK current was observed, but with no significant difference between Gαi1(GTP-γS) and Gαs(GTP-γS), suggesting that their affinities for Gβγ are similar (Figure 5B–5D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the planar lipid bilayer experiments shown in Figure 5B–5D.

claim: Lower Gβγ concentrations following Gαs-coupled receptor stimulation cannot be attributed to sequestration by Gαs(GTP).
source: Thus, lower Gβγ concentrations following Gαs-coupled receptor stimulation cannot be attributed to sequestration by Gαs(GTP).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Gαi1(GTP-γS) and Gαs(GTP-γS) have similar affinities for Gβγ.

claim: The BRET ratio change was small for the β2AR and comparatively large for M2R following GPCR stimulation.
source: Prior to GPCR stimulation, N-Luc intensity and BRET ratio were nearly constant and approximately similar in magnitude in all experiments (Figure 6B–6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and Table 1). Following GPCR stimulation the BRET ratio change was small for the β2AR and comparatively large for M2R.
evidence: This is directly observed in the BRET experiments shown in Figure 6B–6C.

claim: Gβγ-dissociation from Gα is much greater for the Gαi-coupled receptor (D2R) compared to the Gαs-coupled receptor (β1AR).
source: Similar experiments were also carried out with the Gαi-coupled dopamine receptor (D2R), which activates GIRK (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), and the Gαs-coupled β1AR, which does not. Again, we observe that Gβγ-dissociation from Gα is much greater for the Gαi-coupled receptor (Figure 6D–6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–2D, and Table 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the BRET experiments shown in Figure 6D–6E.

claim: The Gαi-coupled receptors M2R and D2R generate more rapid Gβγ release than the Gαs-coupled receptors β1AR and β2AR due to a higher intrinsic turnover rate.
source: We conclude from these experiments that the Gαi-coupled receptors M2R and D2R generate more rapid Gβγ release than the Gαs-coupled receptors β1AR and β2AR due to a higher intrinsic turnover rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the BRET experiments measuring Gβγ dissociation from Gα.

claim: The observation that G protein over-expression increases levels of stimulated Gβγ in cells implies that the k12 transition is to some extent rate-limiting under physiological G protein conditions.
source: In our experiments, the observation that G protein over-expression increases levels of stimulated Gβγ in cells (Figure 3 and Figure 4B) implies that the k12 transition is to some extent rate-limiting under physiological G protein conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that G protein overexpression increases Gβγ generation.

claim: A single molecule study concluded that complex formation between activated receptor and G protein trimer (i.e. the k12 transition) was rate-limiting.
source: A single molecule study of the α2 adrenergic receptor (α2AR; a Gαi-coupled GPCR) also concluded that complex formation between activated receptor and G protein trimer (i.e. the k12 transition) was rate-limiting (Sungkaworn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: k12 for the β2AR was ten times smaller than for the α2AR.
source: Furthermore, the same study found that k12 for the β2AR was ten times smaller than for the α2AR.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: GPCR density over the entire membrane of atrial cardiac myocytes and in CHO cells is approximately 5 µm−2.
source: GPCR density over the entire membrane of atrial cardiac myocytes and in CHO cells is approximately 5 µm−2 (Nenasheva et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: G protein signaling occurs within 'hotspots' that cover about 10% of the membrane surface.
source: However, G protein signaling occurs within 'hotspots' that we estimate to cover about 10% of the membrane surface (Sungkaworn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The modeled time course of GIRK activation falls within the experimental range observed in SAN cells.
source: When the reaction is switched on (i.e. ligand stimulation) at t = 0 by changing k12 from 0 to 0.2 µm2 molecule−1 sec−1 (Sungkaworn et al., 2017), Gβγ concentration increases (along with time-dependent concentration changes of other components) and GIRK channels activate to a steady state value within a few seconds following a time course similar to M2R stimulated GIRK currents in SAN cells (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). We note that time courses vary from cell to cell, but that the modeled time course falls within the experimental range.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the kinetic model output to experimental data in Figure 7B.

claim: Lower concentrations of Gβγ are predicted when k12 is reduced ten times to model the β2AR receptor.
source: To model the β2AR receptor we reduced k12 ten times, consistent with Sungkaworn et al, leaving all other quantities the same. Lower concentrations of Gβγ are predicted and along with significantly less GIRK activation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the kinetic model shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A steep dependence of GIRK activation on k12 magnitude occurs right around the experimentally determined value for the Gαi-coupled receptor turnover rate constant.
source: Figure 7C displays in greater detail calculated GIRK-(Gβγ)4 concentration (i.e. channel activation) as a function of k12 magnitude. A steep dependence occurs right around the experimentally determined value for the Gαi-coupled receptor turnover rate constant (Sungkaworn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the kinetic model shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The model predicts that higher rates of G protein turnover catalyzed by Gαi-coupled compared to Gαs-coupled GPCRs can account for Gβγ specificity.
source: Thus, the model predicts that higher rates of G protein turnover catalyzed by Gαi-coupled compared to Gαs-coupled GPCRs can account for Gβγ specificity.
evidence: This is the conclusion from the kinetic modeling.

claim: Partial agonists activate GPCRs with reduced efficacy compared to full agonists.
source: Partial agonists by definition activate GPCRs with reduced efficacy compared to full agonists (McKinney et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: For the β2AR, the distinction between partial and full agonist action lies in the magnitude of k12, its value being smaller for partial agonists.
source: A study recently concluded that for the β2AR, the distinction between partial and full agonist action lies in the magnitude of k12, its value being smaller for partial agonists (Gregorio et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: When the partial agonists oxotremorine and pilocarpine are used to stimulate M2R, reduced GIRK currents are associated with reduced BRET signals for Gβγ-Venus binding to GIRK-NLuc.
source: We think this conclusion likely applies to M2R as well, based on the following observations. When the partial agonists oxotremorine (Oxo) and pilocarpine (Pilo) are used to stimulate M2R, reduced GIRK currents are associated with reduced BRET signals for Gβγ-Venus binding to GIRK-NLuc (blue symbols in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–1D.

claim: When amounts of available Gαi1 are increased, the partial agonist Oxo gives rise to a BRET signal as strong as that of ACh.
source: Furthermore, when amounts of available Gαi1 are increased (so that more Gαi1(GDP)βγ-Venus can form), the partial agonist Oxo gives rise to a BRET signal as strong as that of ACh (orange symbols in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the BRET experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: k12 can explain the difference in agonists versus partial agonists as well as the fundamental difference between M2R and βARs with respect to their ability to activate GIRK channels.
source: These results are explicable on the basis of the G protein trimer-GPCR on-rate determining the efficacy of different agonists. Thus, k12 can explain the difference in agonists versus partial agonists as well as the fundamental difference between M2R and βARs with respect to their ability to activate GIRK channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial agonist experiments and kinetic modeling.

claim: k12 is rate limiting under physiological G protein concentrations, and its magnitude determines differential rates of Gβγ generation.
source: In the model we present, k12, is rate limiting under physiological G protein concentrations, and its magnitude determines differential rates of Gβγ generation.
evidence: This is the conclusion from the kinetic modeling and experimental data.

claim: M2R catalyzes the generation of Gβγ at a higher rate than β2AR, thus achieving higher concentrations of Gβγ to activate GIRK.
source: The essential conclusion of this study is that M2R catalyzes the generation of Gβγ at a higher rate than β2AR, thus achieving higher concentrations of Gβγ to activate GIRK.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: The concentrations of Gαs(GTP) generated by β2AR are sufficient to stimulate the downstream-amplified Gαs pathway and speed heart rate.
source: The concentrations of Gαs(GTP) generated by β2AR are obviously sufficient to stimulate the downstream-amplified Gαs pathway and speed heart rate, but the lower Gβγ levels generated are insufficient to activate GIRK to a great extent.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that β2AR stimulation increases heart rate but does not activate GIRK.

claim: The higher rate of Gβγ generation by M2R likely stems from an intrinsically higher rate of association with G protein trimer.
source: The higher rate of Gβγ generation by M2R likely stems from an intrinsically higher rate of association with G protein trimer.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by BRET experiments and kinetic modeling.

claim: Endogenous levels of Gα permit Gβγ generation by M2R, but not by β2AR.
source: This conclusion is most easily appreciated through careful inspection of Figure 3D and E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, where it is shown that endogenous levels of Gα (in the presence of expressed Gβγ-Venus to detect Gβγ binding to GIRK) permit Gβγ generation by M2R, but not by β2AR.
evidence: This is directly observed in the BRET experiments shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Over-expression of Gα and Gβγ increases the rate of Gβγ generation in both M2R and β2AR cases.
